chapters.1: Generations after Jacob's family settled in Egypt, the Israelites have multiplied greatly, and a new Pharaoh grows afraid of their numbers. He forces them into harsh slave labor and orders Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys, but the midwives, fearing God, refuse, so Pharaoh commands that all Hebrew baby boys be thrown into the Nile.
chapters.2: A Levite woman hides her infant son in a basket on the Nile to save him from Pharaoh's decree, and he is found and adopted by Pharaoh's own daughter, who names him Moses. As an adult, Moses kills an Egyptian he sees abusing a Hebrew and flees to Midian, where he marries Zipporah, the daughter of the priest Jethro, and settles into life as a shepherd while Israel continues to suffer in Egypt.
chapters.3: While tending sheep near Mount Horeb, Moses sees a bush burning without being consumed, and God speaks to him from it, revealing his name and calling Moses to lead Israel out of Egyptian slavery into the promised land. Moses expresses doubt about his ability to do this, and God promises to be with him and gives him assurance that the Israelites will leave Egypt with wealth from the Egyptians.
chapters.4: Moses raises more objections, so God gives him miraculous signs to perform, including turning his staff into a snake, and when Moses protests that he is not a good speaker, God appoints his brother Aaron to speak on his behalf. Moses returns to Egypt with his family, Aaron meets him and they gather the Israelite elders, and the people believe when they hear that God has taken notice of their suffering.
chapters.5: Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let the Israelites go worship God in the wilderness, but Pharaoh refuses and instead increases their burden, ordering that they must still produce the same quota of bricks without being supplied straw. The Israelite overseers are beaten and blame Moses and Aaron, leaving Moses to cry out to God in frustration that things have only gotten worse.
chapters.6: God reaffirms his covenant promise to Moses and his plan to free Israel, restating his identity and intention to bring them to Canaan despite Moses' discouragement. The chapter then gives the family lines of Reuben, Simeon, and especially Levi in detail, tracing the ancestry of Moses and Aaron down through Levi, Kohath, and Amram.
chapters.7: God tells Moses that Pharaoh's heart will be hardened and that Aaron will serve as his spokesman and "prophet." Aaron's staff turns into a snake before Pharaoh and swallows the magicians' staffs, but Pharaoh remains unmoved, so the first plague begins as Aaron strikes the Nile and turns its water into blood, killing the fish and making the water undrinkable.
chapters.8: God sends the plague of frogs to overwhelm Egypt, and after Pharaoh pleads for relief, Moses prays and the frogs die off, but Pharaoh again hardens his heart. Next come swarms of lice and then flies that plague the Egyptians but spare the Israelites in Goshen, with Pharaoh repeatedly offering concessions and then reneging once each plague lifts.
chapters.9: A plague kills Egypt's livestock while sparing Israel's, followed by a plague of boils on people and animals, yet Pharaoh's heart remains hard. God then sends a devastating hailstorm mixed with fire that destroys crops and kills anything left out in the fields, leading Pharaoh to briefly confess his sin before again refusing to release the Israelites.
chapters.10: God sends a locust plague that devours everything the hail left, prompting Pharaoh's own officials to urge him to relent, and he almost agrees before reneging over Moses' insistence on bringing all the people, flocks, and herds. A plague of thick darkness covers the land for three days, after which Pharaoh angrily banishes Moses from his presence, threatening him with death if he returns.
chapters.11: God tells Moses this will be the final and most severe plague: the death of every firstborn in Egypt, which will finally force Pharaoh to drive the Israelites out completely. Moses warns Pharaoh of what is coming, and the chapter notes that the Israelites were instructed to ask the Egyptians for silver and gold before leaving.
chapters.12: God institutes the Passover, instructing each household to sacrifice a lamb and mark their doorposts with its blood so the plague of death on Egypt's firstborn will pass over them, and establishes the ongoing festival of unleavened bread to commemorate this night. At midnight the plague strikes every Egyptian household, and a grief-stricken Pharaoh finally lets the Israelites leave; roughly 600,000 men plus women and children depart after 430 years in Egypt.
chapters.13: Moses instructs the Israelites to dedicate their firstborn sons and animals to God and to keep the feast of unleavened bread as a lasting reminder of the exodus from Egypt. As Israel sets out, Moses carries Joseph's bones with them, and God leads the people by a pillar of cloud during the day and a pillar of fire by night.
chapters.14: With Pharaoh's army in pursuit, the Israelites find themselves trapped against the Red Sea and panic, but Moses assures them God will save them. God parts the sea so Israel crosses on dry ground, and when the Egyptian chariots follow, the waters crash back down and destroy Pharaoh's entire army, leading Israel to trust in God and in Moses.
chapters.15: Moses and the Israelites sing a triumphant song celebrating God's victory over Pharaoh's army at the Red Sea, and Miriam leads the women in celebration with timbrels and dancing. The people then journey into the wilderness, complain of bitter water at Marah, which God sweetens, and arrive at Elim, where they find water and palm trees.
chapters.16: As food runs short in the wilderness, the people complain bitterly to Moses and Aaron, so God provides quail in the evening and a bread-like substance called manna each morning, giving clear instructions to gather only enough for each day except before the Sabbath, when a double portion is to be collected. The Israelites eat manna throughout their forty years in the wilderness, and a portion is kept as a memorial.
chapters.17: The people again complain of no water, so God has Moses strike a rock at Horeb, producing water for them to drink at a place called Massah and Meribah because of their quarreling. Amalek then attacks Israel, and Joshua leads Israel's forces to victory while Moses, with Aaron and Hur's help, holds up his hands in prayer throughout the battle.
chapters.18: Moses' father-in-law Jethro visits, rejoices to hear what God has done for Israel, and offers sacrifices with Moses and Aaron. Seeing Moses exhausted from judging every dispute among the people alone, Jethro advises him to appoint capable men as judges over smaller groups, handling only the hardest cases himself, and Moses follows this advice.
chapters.19: Israel arrives at Mount Sinai, and God proposes a covenant: if they obey him and keep his commands, they will be his treasured, holy people. The people agree, and God tells Moses to prepare them through consecration and washing for his dramatic appearance on the mountain, which comes with thunder, lightning, smoke, and trumpet blasts as God descends in fire.
chapters.20: God speaks the Ten Commandments directly to the people, covering exclusive worship of God, avoiding idols and misuse of God's name, keeping the Sabbath, honoring parents, and prohibitions against murder, adultery, theft, false testimony, and covetousness. Terrified by the thunder and smoke, the people ask Moses to be their mediator, and God gives additional instructions about building simple altars.
chapters.21: This chapter lays out case laws covering the treatment of Hebrew servants and their release after six years, penalties for violence resulting in death or injury, and the principle of "eye for eye" retribution for serious harm. It also addresses responsibility for injuries caused by animals like a goring ox, applying consistent standards of justice to these everyday situations.
chapters.22: This chapter continues Israel's civil laws, covering restitution for theft of livestock, liability for damage from fire or grazing animals, and rules about borrowed or entrusted property. It also includes protections for vulnerable groups such as foreigners, widows, and orphans, prohibitions on charging interest to the poor, and other ethical and religious regulations.
chapters.23: This chapter gives further laws about honest testimony, impartial justice, fair treatment of enemies' animals, and rest for the land every seventh year. It also establishes Israel's three annual pilgrimage festivals and promises that God's angel will go before Israel to drive out the nations of Canaan as long as Israel avoids their gods.
chapters.24: Moses, Aaron, and seventy elders go partway up Mount Sinai, and the people formally commit to obey all God's words and laws after Moses reads them aloud, sealing the covenant with sacrificial blood. Moses then ascends further into the mountain alone, entering a cloud of God's glory for forty days and nights to receive further instructions and the stone tablets.
chapters.25: God gives detailed instructions for a freewill offering of materials and for building the tabernacle, starting with the ark of the covenant overlaid with gold and topped by a mercy seat with two golden cherubim. Instructions follow for the table for showbread and a golden lampstand (menorah) with its branches shaped like almond blossoms, all to be made exactly according to the pattern God shows Moses.
chapters.26: This chapter details the construction of the tabernacle's structure itself: its linen and goat-hair curtains, the wooden frame boards overlaid with gold and set in silver sockets, and the veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place where the ark would rest. Precise measurements and materials are given for every component.
chapters.27: Instructions continue for the bronze altar of burnt offering and its utensils, followed by specifications for the surrounding courtyard with its linen hangings and bronze-sheathed pillars. The chapter closes with instructions for pure olive oil to keep lamps burning continually in the tabernacle.
chapters.28: God instructs that Aaron and his sons be set apart as priests, with detailed designs for Aaron's sacred garments: an ephod, a breastplate set with twelve gemstones representing Israel's tribes and containing the Urim and Thummim, a blue robe with gold bells and pomegranates on its hem, a turban with a gold plate reading "Holiness to the Lord," and simple garments for his sons.
chapters.29: This chapter describes the week-long ordination ceremony for Aaron and his sons, involving washing, special garments, anointing oil, and the sacrifice of a bull and rams, with specific blood rituals to consecrate them and the altar. It also establishes a daily routine of morning and evening offerings to be maintained perpetually at the tabernacle.
chapters.30: Instructions are given for a golden incense altar, a census tax of half a shekel per person to fund the tabernacle service, a bronze basin for priestly washing, and a precisely formulated holy anointing oil and incense that are reserved exclusively for sacred use, with a death penalty for anyone who copies them for ordinary purposes.
chapters.31: God appoints Bezaleel and Aholiab, gifted craftsmen filled with divine skill, to lead the construction of the tabernacle and its furnishings. God reiterates the command to keep the Sabbath as a perpetual sign of the covenant, and at the end of these instructions gives Moses the two stone tablets of the Ten Commandments, written by God's own hand.
chapters.32: While Moses is on the mountain, the impatient people pressure Aaron into making a golden calf idol to worship, provoking God's anger; Moses intercedes and persuades God not to destroy the nation. Coming down and finding the idolatrous celebration, Moses shatters the stone tablets in anger, destroys the calf, and has the Levites execute roughly three thousand people involved in the rebellion.
chapters.33: God tells Moses the people must leave for Canaan but, because of their rebellion, says he himself will not travel in their midst, grieving the people. Moses pleads for God's continued presence and intimate relationship, and God agrees to go with them personally, allowing Moses to see a partial glimpse of his glory while hidden in a rock, since no one can see God's face and live.
chapters.34: God has Moses cut new stone tablets and renews the covenant, revealing himself as merciful, gracious, and faithful, yet also just toward sin, while again warning against alliances or intermarriage with Canaan's peoples that could lead Israel into idolatry. Moses spends another forty days on the mountain, and when he comes down his face is radiant from being in God's presence, so he wears a veil when not speaking directly to the people.
chapters.35: Moses reminds the people to keep the Sabbath and then relays God's instructions for building the tabernacle, inviting anyone willing to contribute materials like gold, fine fabrics, and wood. The people respond with overwhelming generosity, and Moses announces that Bezaleel and Aholiab have been specially equipped by God to lead the skilled craftsmen in the work.
chapters.36: So much material is donated that the craftsmen have to ask Moses to stop the people from bringing more. Bezaleel, Aholiab, and their skilled workers then begin constructing the tabernacle's curtains, coverings, and the wooden frame with its boards, bars, and sockets exactly as instructed.
chapters.37: Bezaleel constructs the sacred furnishings for the interior of the tabernacle: the gold-covered ark of the covenant with its mercy seat and cherubim, the table for the showbread, the ornate golden lampstand, and the altar of incense, along with the holy anointing oil and incense.
chapters.38: Work continues with the construction of the bronze altar of burnt offering and its utensils, the bronze basin made from mirrors donated by the women, and the linen hangings and pillars enclosing the courtyard. The chapter closes with an accounting of the large quantities of gold, silver, and bronze used for the entire project.
chapters.39: The skilled workers complete Aaron's priestly garments exactly as specified, including the ephod, the jeweled breastplate, the blue robe, and the gold plate reading "Holiness to the Lord." When all the tabernacle's components are finished and brought to Moses, he inspects everything, finds it done exactly as God commanded, and blesses the people for their work.
chapters.40: God instructs Moses on how and when to assemble the tabernacle and its furnishings and to anoint and consecrate Aaron and his sons as priests. Moses sets everything up exactly as commanded, and once the work is complete, a cloud covers the tabernacle and the glory of the Lord fills it so powerfully that even Moses cannot enter, with the cloud afterward guiding Israel's movements through the wilderness.
